text: Make people an offer so good they would feel stupid saying no.
context: Subtitle and thesis of the book. In the origin story he credits the sentence to mentor Travis Jones, then spends the book showing how to build that offer.
A line he uses to train sales teams: name the prospect's pain accurately and they will almost always buy.

text: The point of good writing is for the reader to understand. The point of good persuasion is for the prospect to feel understood.
context: A pro tip separating clear prose from persuasion that makes the buyer feel seen.

text: Getting people to buy is not the objective of a business. Making money is.
context: His case against cutting price to win the sale.

text: Those who pay the most, pay the most attention.
context: Premium price as a way to raise the buyer's investment and follow-through.

text: People want to buy expensive things. They just need a reason.
context: Price high enough to signal a different category, then give the buyer a reason to believe it.

text: When you raise your price, you increase the value the consumer receives without changing anything else about your product.
context: Price as a signal, illustrated with a taste test in which the same wine was rated higher when it was labeled expensive.

text: The best companies in the world focus all their attention on the bottom side of the equation. Making things immediate, seamless, and effortless.
context: Dream outcome and likelihood sit on top of his value equation; time delay and effort sit on the bottom, and the best operators shrink the bottom.

text: No offer? No business. No life.
context: The bottom of his ladder from a missing offer to a Grand Slam Offer, which he says buys freedom.

text: Advertising, the process of making known, lets strangers know about the stuff you sell.
context: His plain definition of advertising: strangers can buy only what they know exists.

text: It's hard to be poor with leads bangin' down your door.
context: The opening line, which he calls a Hormozi family jingle.
Podcast argument that enough repetitions turn success from chance into math.

text: You have to do so much work, so many repetitions that it would be unreasonable to not be successful.
context: The practical test he pairs with volume: pick a number of repetitions at which failure would be unreasonable, then do the work.

text: If you can just do something consistently, you beat everyone.
context: His claim that a steady cadence outperforms people who quit or leave long gaps between attempts.
